performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: “Gnomus”, marked Vivo, is the first movement of Pictures at an Exhibition and depicts a gnome in the form of a wooden nutcracker. Rapid figures in the low strings alternate with woodwind passages, and the music breaks off abruptly several times.

sections.label: A · Vivo, low strings, broken phrases
sections.mNote: Short rapid phrases end on held notes or rests.

sections.label: B · Descending woodwind phrase
sections.mNote: The descending phrase passes to celesta above swooping strings.

sections.label: C · Heavy theme in the wind
sections.mNote: Slower phrases alternate with the rapid figure from the opening.

sections.label: D · Strings with wind melody
sections.mNote: The bass descends by semitones beneath the octave melody.

sections.label: B′ · Descending phrase, muted brass
sections.mNote: The descending phrase returns above low trills.

sections.label: Coda · Velocissimo final run
sections.mNote: At Velocissimo the run ends on an E♭ minor chord.

cues.title: Opening phrases, low strings and woodwinds
cues.text: Low strings and woodwinds play a short, irregular phrase and stop on a held note. A second phrase follows and also stops. Mussorgsky writes fermatas over both notes and rests.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 1–18; orchestral scoring: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hartmann’s nutcracker toy
cues.text: Hartmann’s gnome was a wooden nutcracker made to hang on the Artists’ Club tree, and nuts went into its mouth.
cues.evidence: Stasov’s description of Hartmann’s toy is quoted by Michael Steinberg: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition. The interrupted phrases and fermatas are in Lamm’s piano edition.

cues.title: Meno mosso, chromatic bass
cues.text: Mussorgsky marks this passage Meno mosso. The wind theme is played over the strings, and the bass descends by semitones. In Lamm’s piano edition the passage covers bars 60–71, with the melody in octaves.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 60–71, octave melody and descending chromatic bass; strings and wind theme: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final run, bars 93–99
cues.text: Another fermata follows, and then the final run. Mussorgsky marks it velocissimo and con tutta forza, as fast as possible and with all possible force. The piece ends on an E♭ minor chord.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 93–99, including velocissimo, con tutta forza and final E♭ minor chord: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/gnomus.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Fermata rest before the descending phrase
transitions.from: A · Vivo, low strings, broken phrases
transitions.how: A whole bar of rest under a fermata separates the opening figures from the descending phrase, with a low E♭ sounding beneath it. In Ravel’s orchestration the new line begins in the upper woodwinds. Celesta and strings then join, the strings playing sliding figures.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 17–28; woodwinds, celesta and strings: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: Change to four beats, heavier tempo
transitions.to: C · Heavy theme in the wind
transitions.how: After another fermata, the metre changes from three beats to four. The marking is Poco meno mosso, pesante, slower and heavy, and the bass leaps from E♭ to A. The broad wind tune is set repeatedly against the quick three-beat figure of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 37–55, changes of metre and tempo, E♭–A bass leap; heavy wind idea: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Chromatic bass descent in the Meno mosso
transitions.from: C · Heavy theme in the wind
transitions.how: In the following Meno mosso the tune is expanded into high octaves. Beneath it the bass descends chromatically through E♭, D♭ and C. In Ravel’s orchestration the melody is given to the wind, set against the strings.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 60–71; orchestration: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: Low trills and accelerando
transitions.how: The broad octave tune breaks off. Three-beat bars return, with low trills alternating between E♭ and A. Over them the earlier descending phrase returns, followed by muted brass. At Poco a poco accelerando the tempo gradually increases.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 72–89: E♭ and A trills, three-beat metre and accelerando; muted brass: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia guide.

transitions.title: Fermata before the final run
transitions.how: A forceful A♭ minor chord (A♭–C♭–E♭) takes an added F♭ and stops under a fermata. The final run follows, marked velocissimo, and rises to E♭ minor. One short chord and a rest end the movement.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 90–99: A♭–C♭–E♭ chord with added F♭, fermata and final E♭ minor chord; Mutopia transcription.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (2:43; this file is 2:41), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified; the uploader of the Commons file (Raul654) is not assumed to be one.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Upload dates are not transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No processing is disclosed. The access file is a Wikimedia MP3 derivative of the uploaded Ogg Vorbis file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: Composer who could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
